person.name: John_von_Neumann
person.summary: John von Neumann was a Hungarian-born American mathematician whose work shaped quantum mechanics, game theory, nuclear weapons research, and electronic computing. He taught at the Institute for Advanced Study and helped establish the stored-program design used by modern computers.

conclusion: John von Neumann’s mathematical formulation of quantum mechanics remains central to advanced physics education and research. Economists, political scientists, biologists, and military analysts use forms of game theory developed from Theory of Games and Economic Behavior. The EDVAC report and the IAS machine project helped spread stored-program computer design, which became the model for many later electronic computers.

events.title: Birth in Budapest
events.description: John von Neumann was born into a wealthy, non-observant Jewish family in Budapest, Kingdom of Hungary. His father, Max von Neumann, was a banker with a doctorate in law. His mother, Margaret Kann, raised John with his younger brothers Michael and Nicholas in the family’s apartment above the Kann-Heller offices.

non-observant Jewish.explanation: The family was Jewish by background but did not actively practice the religion. Von Neumann was later baptized a Catholic in 1930.

events.title: Studies at Fasori
events.description: In 1914, John von Neumann entered the Lutheran Fasori Evangélikus Gimnasium, a secondary school in Budapest. Eugene Wigner was one year ahead of him at the school. The two became friends, and von Neumann benefited from its strong mathematics instruction.

events.title: Publishes Set Theory Papers
events.description: John von Neumann published two major mathematics papers at age 19. His second paper gave a modern definition of ordinal numbers, extending the study of ordered sets into infinite sequences.

events.title: Completes Two Degrees
events.description: John von Neumann received a chemical-engineering degree from ETH Zurich in 1926. He also completed a mathematics doctorate at the University of Budapest with summa cum laude honors. His thesis set out a formal system of basic rules for [[Cantor's set theory|set theory]].

Cantor's set theory.explanation: Set theory studies collections of objects and the rules for reasoning about them. It became a central foundation for modern mathematics.

events.background:
His father wanted him to enter industry and asked the engineer Theodore von Kármán to steer him away from mathematics. They settled on chemical engineering as a practical career. He first took a two-year, non-degree chemistry course at the University of Berlin. He then passed the ETH Zurich entrance examination in September 1923. He pursued the Budapest mathematics work at the same time. His doctoral program was at Pázmány Péter University, the institution now known as the University of Budapest.

The doctoral research grew from a problem that had shaken efforts to make set theory a secure basis for mathematics. Bertrand Russell's paradox involved the collection of all collections that do not include themselves. Von Neumann's 1925 thesis developed two ways to rule out such self-containing collections. One was the axiom of foundation. It required sets to be built upward in an ordered sequence. A set belonging to another set had to occur earlier in that sequence. The rule barred a set from belonging to itself.

His second device distinguished sets from classes. A set was a class that belonged to other classes. A proper class did not belong to other classes. Under this approach, the class of all sets that do not belong to themselves could be discussed without treating it as a set. He also introduced inner models to argue that adding the axiom of foundation did not create contradictions. These tools later became central to the mathematical study of sets.

A Rockefeller Foundation grant then took him to the University of Göttingen to study with David Hilbert. Hermann Weyl recalled walks after class during the winter of 1926–1927 with von Neumann and Emmy Noether through Göttingen's cold, rain-soaked streets. They discussed hypercomplex number systems and their representations.

events.title: Begins Lecturing in Berlin
events.description: John von Neumann began lecturing at the University of Berlin in 1928. He became a [[Privatdozent]], a teacher qualified to lecture independently after completing a habilitation. He was the youngest person elected to that rank in the university’s history.

Privatdozent.explanation: In the German university system, a Privatdozent could teach independently after completing a habilitation. The rank did not necessarily carry a salaried professorship.

events.title: Begins Teaching at Princeton
events.description: John von Neumann left the University of Hamburg for Princeton in 1929. Princeton University appointed him a visiting lecturer in mathematical physics, the use of mathematics to study physical problems.

events.title: Formalizes Quantum Mechanics
events.description: John von Neumann published Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik in Berlin in 1932. The book grew from his work on spectral theory and gave quantum mechanics a mathematical framework based on [[Hilbert space|Hilbert spaces]] and [[operator|operators]].

Hilbert space.explanation: A Hilbert space is a complete mathematical space that generalizes ordinary geometric space and allows quantum states to be represented as vectors.

operator.explanation: An operator is a mathematical rule that acts on a state or function. In quantum mechanics, operators represent measurable physical quantities such as position and energy.

events.background:
Quantum mechanics had given physicists successful rules for calculating atomic phenomena, while the mathematics of infinite-dimensional spaces was still being built. In papers from 1929 through 1932, von Neumann developed spectral theory for operators in Hilbert space. He gave the general form of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. He also separated Hermitian operators from self-adjoint operators. That distinction let him describe every Hermitian operator extending a given one. It addressed operators that were unbounded, a case that arose in quantum mechanics and lay beyond earlier spectral results.

A technical obstacle concerned weak topologies, which describe a weaker sense of convergence than ordinary distance. Mathematicians had found that sequences alone could not produce a satisfactory theory of these topologies. Von Neumann outlined a route around the problem. He introduced locally convex spaces and topological vector spaces. He also applied Hausdorff's newer topological ideas to Hilbert spaces. Boundedness and total boundedness, concepts he formulated in that setting, remained in use.

The volume gathered this operator work into a single mathematical treatment of quantum theory. Its account of spectral theory stood beside monographs by Marshall Stone and Stefan Banach among the first books on Hilbert-space theory. The same research program led von Neumann to the study of rings of operators, later called von Neumann algebras. His early ideas for those algebras already existed by 1930. He began their sustained study several years later after meeting F. J. Murray.

The book's framework became a standard point of reference for mathematical physics. It joined earlier results on abstract Hilbert spaces with a systematic account of the operators used in quantum theory. Von Neumann continued to extend spectral theory through direct integrals of Hilbert spaces and through work on operator algebras.

events.title: Joins the Institute for Advanced Study
events.description: John von Neumann accepted a tenured professorship at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton in 1933. The new institution brought scholars together for research free from regular teaching duties.

images.caption: Fuld Hall, Institute for Advanced Study
images.creator: Zeete

events.title: Marries Klára Dán
events.description: John von Neumann married Klára Dán in Princeton on November 17, 1938. Dán was a Hungarian woman whom he had met at a casino in Monte Carlo.

events.title: Works at Los Alamos
events.description: John von Neumann joined the [[Manhattan Project|Manhattan Project]] at J. Robert Oppenheimer’s Los Alamos Laboratory in 1943. He used hydrodynamics and shock-wave calculations to model [[explosive lenses]], shaped charges that compressed plutonium for an implosion bomb.

locations.name_modern: Los Alamos, New Mexico, United States

Manhattan Project.explanation: The Manhattan Project was the secret United States-led World War II program that developed the first atomic bombs.

explosive lenses.explanation: Explosive lenses use carefully shaped charges to focus an explosive wave inward. They were essential to the implosion design used with plutonium.

events.title: Publishes Game Theory
events.description: John von Neumann and economist Oskar Morgenstern published Theory of Games and Economic Behavior in Princeton in 1944. The book used mathematics to study strategic choices when each participant’s outcome depends on the choices of others.

event_class.title: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior
event_class.impact: The book is credited with founding the field of game theory and brought mathematical analysis into economics and strategic studies.

events.background:
Economic theory in Vienna had already led Morgenstern to a problem about prediction. His 1935 article Perfect Foresight and Economic Equilibrium brought a response from the mathematician Eduard Čech, who pointed him to von Neumann’s 1928 paper Zur Theorie der Gesellschaftsspiele. That earlier paper supplied a mathematical treatment of games between players with opposed interests. Morgenstern arrived at Princeton in 1938 as a visitor. Adolf Hitler’s annexation of Austria took place during the visit. Morgenstern remained in the United States and joined Princeton’s economics faculty. He spent time at the Institute for Advanced Study, where the two men began their collaboration.

The earlier work centered on two-person zero-sum games. In such a game, one player’s gain equals the other’s loss. The minimax theorem gave each player a way to choose a strategy that protected against the opponent’s best possible reply. The result allowed players to use mixed strategies, meaning calculated probabilities assigned to several available moves. The collaboration carried this treatment into economic questions and treated political and military decisions as strategic problems too.

The work opened new lines of investigation in mathematics and economics. It drew academic and practical interest in strategic decision-making. Morgenstern remained at Princeton through 1970 and later wrote an account of the collaboration in the Journal of Economic Literature. The University of Vienna named Oskar-Morgenstern-Platz for him in 2012. Its Faculty of Business, Economics and Statistics and its Faculty of Mathematics stand there.

events.title: Circulates the EDVAC Report
events.description: John von Neumann circulated First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC on June 30, 1945. He prepared it after discussions with Herman Goldstine, John Mauchly, and J. Presper Eckert at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia. The report proposed an electronic computer that kept instructions and numerical data in the same memory.

images.caption: First Draft of the EDVAC report
images.creator: Paul Sableman

event_class.title: First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC
event_class.impact: The report helped spread the stored-program design that influenced the construction of early electronic digital computers.

events.title: Builds the IAS Machine
events.description: John von Neumann directed an electronic-computer project at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton from 1946. Working with Julian Bigelow and Herman Goldstine, he designed the IAS machine as a stored-program computer for scientific calculation. The project produced an operating machine by 1952.

event_class.title: IAS machine
event_class.description: A stored-program electronic computer using binary arithmetic and random-access memory, built for scientific calculation at Princeton.
event_class.impact: Its design guides the construction of early scientific computers in the United States and Europe.

events.title: Joins the Atomic Energy Commission
events.description: In 1955, John von Neumann joined the United States Atomic Energy Commission, the federal body responsible for atomic energy development. He took part in government decisions concerning atomic energy, nuclear weapons, and national defense research.

events.title: Receives Cancer Diagnosis
events.description: Doctors discovered cancer near John von Neumann’s collarbone in 1955. Its primary site could not be determined with certainty.

events.title: Death at Walter Reed
events.description: John von Neumann’s cancer had spread as his illness advanced. He asked a priest for the [[last rites|Roman Catholic last rites]] and remained frightened of death. He died at Walter Reed Army Medical Hospital in Washington, D.C., on February 8, 1957.

images.caption: Walter Reed Army Hospital, Washington, D.C.
images.creator: Highsmith, Carol M., 1946-, photographer

last rites.explanation: Last rites are Catholic prayers and sacraments offered to a person facing serious illness or death. They can include confession, anointing, and Communion.

events.background:
In the mid-1950s, national security work occupied a large share of his time. He chaired Defense Department committees, including the Strategic Missile Evaluation Committee and the ICBM Scientific Advisory Committee. He served on the Atomic Energy Commission, which directed the country’s atomic-energy development. Bernard Schriever and Trevor Gardner worked with him on the first American intercontinental ballistic missile programs. Colleagues regarded him as the nation’s foremost authority on nuclear weapons. His house on Westcott Road in Princeton had long been a gathering place for the local academic community. Stanisław Ulam, his closest American friend, recalled a mind that often found an answer after a night’s sleep.

His final public intellectual project grew from the Silliman Lectures at Yale University. The lectures considered the relation between computing machinery and the human nervous system. Klára Dán von Neumann prepared a preface after his death. Yale University Press issued the lectures in 1958 as The Computer and the Brain. The book set the limits of comparison carefully. The brain used a vast network of nerve cells. The early electronic machines then available operated with a far smaller number of elements and at radically different speeds.

Klára had worked directly with the new machines that formed part of that comparison. She programmed MANIAC I at Los Alamos and helped program ENIAC for a pioneering computer weather forecast. She trained a group drawn from the Manhattan Project to store programs as binary code. Her work on the forecast required managing 100,000 punch cards over 32 days. Afterward, she preserved the lectures for publication while continuing a career that had begun in the earliest years of electronic programming.
